name: Niccolò de Franceschi
text: The earliest man the Croatian branch counts as its own. He acted for Guillaume Grimoard — later Pope Urban V — in negotiations between Louis I of Anjou and the Republic of Venice. By a charter given at Buda on 8 March 1359 Louis received him into the hereditary Hungarian-Croatian nobility with arms, for estates around Zadar. Every Zadar and Omiš descent traces to him.
note: The family no longer holds the charter; the claim rests on the Croatian nobiliary literature and on the 1838 submission to the Austrian commission.

name: Andrea dei Franceschi
text: Grand Chancellor of Venice — the highest office a man outside the patriciate could reach, and held for life. At nineteen he went with an embassy to the Hungarian court and wrote up the journey over the Brenner and through the Tyrol; missions to Naples, Rome, Cairo and Constantinople followed, and in 1515 he attended Leo X's entries into Bologna and Florence. He was made a Secretary to the Council of Ten in 1519, given custody of the public library in the Doge's Palace, and in 1528 co-edited an index of the chancery's documents. Elected Grand Chancellor on 15 September 1529, he appeared in the Collegio in crimson robes with ducal open sleeves and was told by Doge Andrea Gritti, after a run of disastrous appointments, to put the Chancery in order. He did, and held the post for twenty-three years.
note: Deborah Howard, «Titian's Portraits of Grand Chancellor Andrea de' Franceschi». He drew his will in 1535 and added five codicils, each on 1 March — the Venetian new year — in 1538, 1541, 1545, 1549 and 1551, in perfect chancery script in a parchment booklet. His household in the parish of San Severo was learned; three of his brothers followed him into the Chancery; he left no children. Two Titian portraits were willed to his nephew Hieronimo, who died first. He was given a state funeral in 1552 and buried at Santi Giovanni e Paolo, the doges' church; Sansovino transcribed his tomb slab in the first cloister in 1581, giving his age as seventy-nine. Versions of the portrait are in Detroit, Washington and the Royal Collection.

name: Piero della Francesca
text: Born Piero di Benedetto, son of Benedetto de' Franceschi, a tradesman of the Tuscan Franceschi. He is called after his mother — la Francesca, as she was known by marriage into the family — and he is the reason the name is in every history of the Renaissance. The Urbino diptych puts Federico da Montefeltro and Battista Sforza in profile against a continuous landscape, and puts perspective at the service of two faces.
note: The name is the same name. Whether the Tuscan Franceschi and the Friulian-Istrian De Franceschi share an ancestor is not shown by anything in this archive, and the surname is far too common to assume it.

name: Piero, as the sixteenth century drew him
text: Vasari's Lives gave each artist a woodcut portrait in an ornamental frame. Vasari, who came from Arezzo where Piero's frescoes are, complained that Piero's pupil had taken the credit for his master's books — which is the reason we know Piero wrote them.

name: Girolamo de' Franceschi
text: Born at Capodistria into a family from Udine — the Friulian origin again — he entered the Servites as a boy, took his doctorate in theology at Bologna at nineteen, and was four times vicar general of the reformed Congregation. Appointed bishop of Corone in Greece in 1496, he never went: the see fell to the Turks in 1499, and he stayed with his patron. He died at Udine in 1513 and was buried in the family tomb.

name: Francesco Franceschi
text: A printer who worked in metal rather than wood, which is why his 1565 Orlando Furioso — an engraving before every canto, an engraved frame round every argument — was copied by English publishers a generation later. He also printed music, including Zarlino. Two probable relatives, Giovanni Antonio de' Franceschi at Palermo and Venice and Giacomo Franceschi of Venice, printed music too.

name: Domenico de' Franceschi
text: Another Venetian press under the name. He published the woodcut procession of Süleyman the Magnificent going to the mosque (1563), Charles V's storming of La Goletta near Tunis, and a Battle of Lepanto printed in the year after the battle — news engraving, sold in the street while it was still news.
note: A Goleta sheet is at the Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen.

name: Alessandro de Franceschi OP
text: Bishop of Forlì from 1594. His father was Hananel — Nello — Graziadio da Foligno, a rabbi who on baptism took the name Alessandro Franceschi in homage to Cardinal Alessandro Farnese. The surname in this instance is not descent but conversion: a name chosen, not inherited.

name: Mariano de Franceschi
text: Trained at the Accademia di San Luca and under the Spaniard Baldomero Galofre; debuted at the Amatori e Cultori exhibition in Rome in 1876 with a still life, then turned to landscape and genre. He exhibited at Turin in 1884, at Capri and Rome in 1888, and at Venice.

name: Carlo De Franceschi
text: Born at Moncalvo di Pisino — Gologorica — son of Giuseppe, a smallholder loyal to Austria, and Lambertina Peschle of Volosca. Schooled by the parish priest, then Pazin, Fiume and the seminary at Gorizia; law at Graz, where his anti-Austrian views hardened. He wrote L'Istria: note storiche, and he wrote the letter to Giovanni Kobler that this archive leans on for the family's own account of itself. The Blasonario Giuliano's entry for his family calls him «uno dei più arditi patrioti istriani» — one of the boldest of Istrian patriots — and records that he was Secretary of the Provincial Assembly of Istria.
note: He is this family's historian, and the one who says the family came from Carnia about 1700. He also buried at least four children — see the register of the dead. And he is still cited: Egidio Ivetic writes that for medieval Istria one must rely on Benussi, Carlo De Franceschi and De Vergottini.

name: Camillo De Franceschi
text: Carlo's youngest child, and the one who turned the family's history-writing into a profession. Archivist and historian of Venezia Giulia; he edited the statutes of Labin, the chartulary of Piran, and the study of the Castropola lordship over Pula, and wrote the «Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino» — the documented history of the county his own family lived in — published posthumously in 1964 by his son Carlo. He died an exile at Venice in 1953. The armorial notes him as Commendatore and past President of the Società Istriana di Archeologia e Storia Patria.
note: Still standard. A 2021 doctoral dissertation on Venetian Istria names three figures who «tower» over the field — Bernardo Benussi, Giovanni de Vergottini and Camillo de Franceschi — and quotes Egidio Ivetic that for medieval Istria «ci dobbiamo affidare agli studi di Bernardo Benussi, Carlo De Franceschi e Giovanni De Vergottini»: we have to rely on them. Father and son are both named. And more than standard: the same dissertation notes that Camillo used primary sources «today unavailable due to the detrimental effect of the Second World War and its bloody aftermath in Istria». For some documents his articles are now the only witness. Josip Banić, «Venetian Istria in the Embrace of a Nascent Dominium», CEU 2021.

name: Giovanni — il Zuane — de Franceschi
text: In the Venetian-Ottoman war of 1718 he led volunteers from Piska by way of Vrulja to the siege of Imotski, joined after three days by German and Swiss mercenaries with cannon and horsemen from Sinj. Imotski and Vrgorac were taken and the Dalmatian-Bosnian border was fixed where it still runs. The Republic gave him the estates of Arch-bey Čaušević — land, houses, a mill, a tower on the Vrljika. Kačić-Miošić put the feat in a song.
note: An old family tomb with carved arms stands before the altar of the church at Piska.

name: Giovanni de Franceschi
text: Professor, historian, essayist, travel writer; chancellor to the bishop and honorary canon of Split. He published the monthly La Dalmazia at Zadar and argued in it for an enlightened cosmopolitanism. His poem Dalmatinska vila appeared in 1844.

name: Jean-Marie-Antoine Defrance
text: Écuyer to the Emperor, brigadier general, made a count of the Empire by letters patent of 2 July 1808 at Bayonne. His arms: party azure and gules, cut argent — azure with the sign of the military counts; gules with a golden cock; argent with three azure halberd-irons, two and one.
note: A separate line: the French Defrance, not the Istrian Defranceschi. Included because the surname converges.

name: Jean-Baptiste-Marie Franceschi
text: Brigadier general and aide-de-camp to the King of Spain and the Indies, made a baron of the Empire by letters patent of 23 June 1810. The Corsican Franceschi came from Florence: a Taddeo Franceschi crossed to Corsica early in the fourteenth century, and his descendants served Genoa until Corsica went to France in 1768.

name: Marcantonio de Franceschi
text: Secretary of the Council of Ten in 1567 — the same body Andrea de' Franceschi had served as secretary from 1519 before his election to the Grand Chancellorship. Two men of the name, a generation apart, inside the most secret organ of the Venetian state. He belongs to the Candia and Seghetto branch: the armorial names him in the same entry as the four brothers who gave the Republic a hundred thousand ducats in 1716.

name: Francesco de Franceschi
text: Bishop of Pola in 1424 — the earliest office-holder of the name recorded anywhere in Istria, and a century before the Chancellor. He belonged to the Capodistria family, which the Gravisi manuscript records as originally Venetian, aggregated to the nobility of Pola in 1580, and extinct.
note: Blasonario Giuliano, «Franceschi — Capodistria». That family bore a bent bend charged with a lion passant or.

name: Luca di Nicolò de Franceschi
text: The first of the family whose nobility is actually proved in the registers of the Archive of the Duke of Candia. His father Nicolò was castellan of Castel Milopotamo in 1500. The family had been enrolled in the Cretan nobility earlier than this, but 1488 is where the documents begin — and it is the point at which the Seghetto branch's story stops being tradition and starts being record.
note: Blasonario Giuliano, after Spreti. Everything before 1488 in that family's account of itself — the prefect Feramondo of 474, the flight to Padua, the crossing to Crete between 1211 and 1257 — is tradition.

name: Carlo Prospero Defranceschi
text: Court poet and librettist in the Italian theatres of the Habsburg capitals. He wrote the libretto of Antonio Salieri's «Angiolina, ossia Il matrimonio per sussurro», and styled himself on his title pages «Licenziato de' Dritti» — licensed in law — and «Riducitore del Sacrificio interrotto, e d'Amore e Psiche». His «Il Principe d'Itaca», a dramma eroicomico reduced from the German for the use of the Italian theatre, was staged at the new theatre in Prague in 1797 under Domenico Guardasoni, the impresario who had commissioned «La clemenza di Tito» from Mozart six years earlier in the same house.
note: Two printed libretti carry his name: the Prague «Principe d'Itaca» of 1797, in the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, and the Florence edition of «Angiolina» of 1815, which credits «Libretto by C. P. Defranceschi». No connection to this family is claimed.

name: Ante Defranceschi
text: Author of «Metoda početnoga čitanja i pisanja te put do slobodnih sastavaka» — a method of first reading and writing, and the road to free composition. It is a teachers' manual: how to bring a child from letters to writing something of their own. He wrote it in Croatian, under the Croatian spelling of the name, in the decade when this family's own children at Crikvenica were being taught to read.
note: Held at the Internet Archive. Nothing links him to this line beyond the surname and the country; he is here because he is the only one of the name to have written a book in Croatian.

name: Jean Defranceschi
text: Historian of Corsica and of the French Revolution. His essay «Robespierre et la Corse» stands in the Lille volume «Robespierre: de la Nation artésienne à la République et aux Nations», and argues that the Corsican revolution of 1729–69 — drowned at Ponte Nuovo when Robespierre was eleven — was a live example to the men of 1789, and that Corsica in that year was not yet legally French.
note: A Corsican bearer of the name, and a reminder of how far the patronymic travelled: the family's own map already carries Corsica and a Corsica-to-Genoa marker. No connection to any line on this site.

name: Camillo De Franceschi, in Croatian
text: Camillo's «Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino» — the documented history of the County of Pazin, published posthumously in 1964 — is still the standing authority. Current Croatian scholarship cites it page by page: Elvis Orbanić's study of the bishops of Pićan leans on it a dozen times, and Irma Huić's study of Gračišće opens its bibliography with it. In 2023 it appeared in Croatian as «Povijest Pazinske knežije na temelju isprava», from Josip Turčinović of Pazin.
note: Carlo wrote the history of the province; his son wrote the history of the county; and the county's history is now in the language of the people who live there. It can be bought.
